title: Blood Draws
tag: Venipuncture and specimen collection — patient to labeled tube.

lessons.title: The phlebotomist's role & safety
lessons.lead: Before you ever pick up a needle, you take on two jobs at once: get the right specimen from the right patient, and protect that patient — and yourself — from harm. Everything else in phlebotomy sits on top of these two duties.
objectives: Define the phlebotomist's scope of practice and its limits
Apply standard precautions and correct PPE for every patient encounter
Explain the chain of infection and how technique breaks it
Perform two-identifier patient identification as the top safety duty

sections.h: What your role is — and is not
p: Your job is to collect and label specimens correctly and get them to the lab in good condition. You work within a defined scope of practice: you draw, label, and transport — you do not diagnose, interpret results, or advise on treatment, and you work under supervision and within your role.
That boundary protects patients. When a patient asks what a result means, redirect them to the ordering provider. Knowing the edge of your role is itself a clinical skill.
list: In scope: verify orders, identify the patient, select the site, collect, label at the bedside, transport.
Out of scope: interpreting values, changing orders, giving a diagnosis or prognosis.
Escalate: unexpected reactions, failed draws, or anything outside your training goes to a supervisor or nurse.

note.t: If a task is outside your training or your facility's protocol, stop and ask — practicing beyond your role is a patient-safety risk, not initiative.

p: Standard precautions mean you treat every patient's blood and body fluids as if they are infectious, regardless of diagnosis. You never know a patient's full status, so you protect the same way every time.

Gloves are required for every draw and are changed between every patient — never reused. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene: perform hand hygiene before and after each patient, before gloving and after removing gloves. Dispose of sharps immediately in a puncture-resistant container at the point of use.
list: Hand hygiene before patient contact and before gloving.
Fresh gloves for every patient — one patient, one pair.
Hand hygiene again after glove removal, even if gloves looked intact.
Activate the safety device and drop the sharp in the container without recapping.

note.t: Recapping needles is a leading cause of needlestick injury — engage the safety mechanism and discard immediately instead.

sections.h: The chain of infection and professionalism
p: Infection spreads through a chain: a pathogen, a reservoir, a portal of exit, a mode of transmission, a portal of entry, and a susceptible host. Your technique is designed to break a link — hand hygiene and gloves interrupt transmission, aseptic site prep closes the portal of entry, and safe sharps handling removes the vehicle.

The human side matters just as much. Calm, respectful rapport reduces patient anxiety, which lowers the chance of a vasovagal reaction and makes veins easier to access. Professionalism — introducing yourself, explaining the steps, honesty about a stick — earns the trust that makes the draw go well.

note.t: You cannot remove every link, but breaking any one link stops transmission — which is why simple hand hygiene is the single highest-impact infection-control step.

inter.h: Your single most important safety duty
inter.case: You arrive at the bedside with a printed label and an order for a CBC.
inter.q: Of everything you do at the bedside, which action most directly prevents a serious patient-harm event?

opts.lab: Interpret the result for the patient so they feel informed
opts.fb: Out of scope — you do not interpret results, and this does nothing to prevent harm at collection.

opts.lab: Confirm patient identity using two identifiers before drawing
opts.fb: Correct — accurate patient identification is the phlebotomist's single most important safety duty; a mislabeled specimen can send the wrong result to the wrong patient.

opts.lab: Choose the largest vein you can see
opts.fb: Site selection matters, but it does not protect against the most catastrophic error: drawing or labeling for the wrong patient.

tips: Introduce yourself and explain what you are about to do — a prepared patient is a calmer, easier draw.
Ask the patient to state their full name and date of birth; do not read it to them and wait for a nod.
Keep your sharps container within arm's reach before you start, so you never carry an exposed needle.
mistakes: Reusing one pair of gloves across two patients.
Skipping hand hygiene because gloves 'looked clean.'
Recapping a used needle by hand.
Confirming identity by reading the name aloud and accepting a yes.
takeaways: You collect and label; you do not diagnose or interpret.
Treat all blood as infectious — gloves every patient, hand hygiene before and after.
Good technique breaks a link in the chain of infection.
Two-identifier patient ID is your most important safety duty.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes standard precautions?
opts: Wear extra PPE only for known-positive patients
Treat every patient's blood and body fluids as potentially infectious
Precautions apply only in isolation rooms
quiz.why: Standard precautions assume all blood and body fluids may be infectious, because status is never fully known.

quiz.q: How should gloves be managed between patients?
opts: Reused if they still look intact
Changed between every patient, with hand hygiene before and after
quiz.why: Fresh gloves for each patient plus hand hygiene before and after prevents cross-contamination.

quiz.q: What is the phlebotomist's single most important safety duty?
opts: Accurate patient identification with two identifiers
Interpreting the result for the patient
quiz.why: Correct identification prevents the most catastrophic errors — wrong patient, wrong result.

lessons.title: Venous anatomy for venipuncture
lessons.lead: The vein you choose sets up everything that follows. A confident draw starts with a mental map of the antecubital fossa and a feel for the artery and nerve that share the neighborhood.
objectives: Map the median cubital, cephalic, and basilic veins and rank them by preference
Explain why the basilic vein is the last choice
Distinguish the H-pattern from the M-pattern of superficial veins
Differentiate a vein from an artery and a nerve by feel and response

p: Routine venipuncture targets the antecubital fossa — the crease at the front of the elbow — because the veins there are large, superficial, and relatively fixed. Three veins matter, and they are not interchangeable.
You rank them by a simple logic: how central and well-anchored the vein is, and what dangerous structures lie beneath it.
list: Median cubital vein — first choice. Central, large, and well-anchored, so it barely moves; it also sits away from the artery and nerve.
Cephalic vein — second choice. Lateral, on the thumb side; accessible but tends to roll, so anchor it firmly.
Basilic vein — last choice. Medial, on the little-finger side; used last because the brachial artery and median nerve lie close beneath it.

note.t: Reach for the basilic vein only after the median cubital and cephalic have been ruled out — an errant stick there can hit the brachial artery or median nerve.

p: Superficial antecubital veins are not laid out identically in every arm. Two common distributions are named for the shapes they trace on the skin.

In the H-pattern, the median cubital connects the cephalic and basilic like the crossbar of an H — the most common layout and the reason the median cubital is usually your best target. In the M-pattern, the median antebrachial vein branches into a median cephalic and median basilic, forming an M; here you follow the branch that leads away from the artery and nerve. Reading which pattern you are looking at tells you where to aim.

note.t: Do not assume every arm is an H — palpate the actual course of the vein in front of you before you commit to an angle.

p: Three structures can sit under your fingertip, and only one is your target. A vein is soft, springy, non-pulsatile, and refills when you press and release. An artery pulsates, sits deeper, and refills briskly — if a vessel pulses, do not stick it. A nerve gives no pulse at all, but contact produces a sharp, electric, shooting pain; if the patient reports that, withdraw immediately.

This is why superficial forearm and antecubital veins are the preferred targets: they sit close to the surface, away from major arteries and nerves, so the risk of hitting the wrong structure is lowest.

note.t: Palpate with a fingertip, not your thumb — your thumb has its own pulse and will make a vein feel like an artery.

inter.case: As you advance the needle, the patient yelps with a sudden shooting, electric pain radiating down the forearm.
inter.q: What has most likely happened, and what do you do?

opts.lab: You nicked an artery — apply a warm pack and continue
opts.fb: No — arterial contact gives pulsatile bright-red flash, not electric radiating pain, and you would never continue into it.

opts.lab: You contacted a nerve — withdraw the needle immediately
opts.fb: Correct — sharp, electric, radiating pain signals nerve contact; withdraw at once to avoid lasting injury.

opts.lab: Normal for a deep vein — push a little further
opts.fb: Dangerous — a vein does not cause shooting electric pain; advancing risks permanent nerve damage.

tips: Anchor and feel before you decide — a vein you can palpate beats one you can only see.
Warmth and lowering the arm bring superficial veins up without slapping.
Trace the vein's course with a fingertip so you know if you are looking at an H or an M before you angle in.
mistakes: Going straight for the basilic vein because it looks big.
Sticking a pulsatile vessel — that is an artery.
Ignoring a patient's report of sharp electric pain.
Choosing a vein you can see but cannot feel.
takeaways: Median cubital first, cephalic second, basilic last.
Basilic is last because the brachial artery and median nerve lie beneath it.
Pulsatile = artery; electric shooting pain = nerve; both mean stop.
Superficial antecubital and forearm veins are targeted because they are shallow and away from artery and nerve.

quiz.q: Which antecubital vein is the preferred first choice?
quiz.why: It is central, large, well-anchored, and sits away from the brachial artery and median nerve.

quiz.q: Why is the basilic vein used last?
opts: The brachial artery and median nerve lie close beneath it
quiz.why: Its proximity to the artery and median nerve makes it the highest-risk of the three.

quiz.q: A vessel under your finger pulses steadily. What is it?
quiz.why: Pulsatility signals an artery; cannulating it risks arterial injury.

lessons.title: Tubes, additives & collection systems
lessons.lead: The tube you choose is a chemistry decision, not just a container. Match the needle to the vein and the additive to the test, and half the errors in phlebotomy disappear before you even puncture the skin.
objectives: Identify the components of the evacuated tube system
Select the correct needle gauge for the vein and situation
Match tube-stopper colors to their additives and intended tests
Explain why additive tubes must be inverted immediately after filling

p: The evacuated tube system (ETS) is the standard collection method. It has three parts: a multi-sample needle, a tube holder (adapter), and a vacuum tube. The tube's premeasured vacuum pulls the exact volume of blood it is calibrated for, so the blood-to-additive ratio stays correct.

The multi-sample needle is double-ended: the front bevel enters the vein while a rubber-sleeved back end lets you change tubes without leaking. For fragile or difficult veins, the syringe method gives you manual control over draw speed — you pull gently, then transfer the blood into tubes using a transfer device rather than pushing through the needle.
list: 21G — the standard multisample needle for routine adult venipuncture.
22G — for smaller or more delicate veins.
23G winged (butterfly) set — for hand, fragile, or pediatric veins; the tubing gives you control and a gentler approach.

note.t: Too small a gauge (higher number) can hemolyze the sample by forcing cells through a narrow bore; too large stresses a fragile vein — match the gauge to the vein you actually feel.

p: Each stopper color signals an additive chosen for a specific test. Knowing the color-to-chemistry map is what lets you draw the right tube the first time.

Anticoagulants work by different mechanisms: some bind (chelate) calcium so blood cannot clot, others inhibit the clotting cascade. Serum tubes do the opposite — they help blood clot fully so you can spin off clear serum.
list: Lavender — EDTA: chelates calcium; used for hematology / CBC.
Light blue — sodium citrate: for coagulation studies; the 9:1 blood-to-additive fill ratio is critical — a short draw invalidates the result.
Green — heparin: inhibits thrombin; used for plasma chemistry.
Red (plain) and gold / tiger SST: SST adds a clot activator plus a gel separator; both give serum for chemistry.
Gray — sodium fluoride + potassium oxalate: fluoride inhibits glycolysis to preserve glucose and lactate.

note.t: A light-blue citrate tube must fill completely — the fixed 9:1 ratio means an underfilled tube has too much anticoagulant and will falsely prolong clotting times.

sections.h: Why you invert — and invert gently
p: The moment an additive tube fills, the additive is only coating the wall; it has to mix with the blood to work. You invert the tube gently several times right after filling — a full end-over-end turn per inversion — so the anticoagulant or clot activator distributes evenly.

Skip it and an anticoagulated tube forms microclots, ruining a CBC or coagulation study. Do it too hard and you shear red cells, causing hemolysis that wrecks potassium and other chemistries. Gentle and complete is the target — never shake.

note.t: Inversions are counted per tube type (for example, several for EDTA and citrate) because too few leaves clots and too vigorous a mix causes hemolysis — both reject the sample.

inter.h: Pick the tube for the test
inter.case: You have an order for a CBC on an adult with good antecubital veins.
inter.q: Which tube collects the specimen for a CBC?

opts.lab: Light-blue sodium citrate tube
opts.fb: That is for coagulation studies with a strict 9:1 fill ratio — not hematology.

opts.lab: Lavender EDTA tube
opts.fb: Correct — EDTA chelates calcium and preserves cell morphology, making it the tube for CBC and hematology.

opts.lab: Gray sodium fluoride tube
opts.fb: Fluoride preserves glucose by inhibiting glycolysis; it is not used for a CBC.

tips: Reach for a 23G butterfly on hand veins and fragile or pediatric patients — the tubing lets you approach at a shallow angle with control.
Let each tube fill until the vacuum stops on its own; do not pull it early or the ratio is wrong.
Invert additive tubes immediately, before you set them down, so the additive never gets a chance to sit unmixed.
mistakes: Underfilling a light-blue citrate tube and breaking the 9:1 ratio.
Shaking tubes instead of gently inverting them, causing hemolysis.
Grabbing a gel SST when the assay requires plain serum or plasma.
Using a high-gauge needle on a good vein and hemolyzing the sample.
takeaways: ETS = multi-sample needle + tube holder + vacuum tube.
21G is standard; 22G for small veins; 23G butterfly for fragile/hand/pediatric.
Color codes the additive: lavender EDTA, blue citrate, green heparin, red/gold serum, gray fluoride.
Invert additive tubes gently and completely right after filling — never shake.

quiz.q: Which needle is the standard for routine adult multisample venipuncture?
quiz.why: 21G balances flow and vein safety and is the standard multisample needle.

quiz.q: Why must a light-blue sodium citrate tube be filled completely?
opts: To preserve the 9:1 blood-to-additive ratio for accurate coagulation results
quiz.why: Coagulation testing depends on a fixed 9:1 ratio; underfilling over-anticoagulates the sample.

quiz.q: What does the sodium fluoride in a gray-top tube do?
quiz.why: Fluoride stops cells from consuming glucose, keeping glucose and lactate results accurate.

lessons.refs: CLSI GP41 (2017); manufacturer tube guides; ASCP/NAACLS phlebotomy competencies.

lessons.title: Order of draw
lessons.lead: Fill tubes in the wrong sequence and one tube's additive can contaminate the next — turning a normal patient's results into a false emergency. The CLSI order of draw exists to stop that carryover.
objectives: State the CLSI order of draw from first tube to last
Explain how the sequence prevents additive carryover
Predict the errors caused by drawing tubes out of order
Apply the discard-tube rule when using a butterfly for coagulation

p: As blood passes through the needle, a trace of additive from one tube can cling to the needle and be carried into the next tube. This additive carryover can change results even when the patient is perfectly normal.

The classic example: EDTA carryover falsely raises potassium and lowers calcium, because EDTA is potassium-based and binds calcium. Similarly, any additive dragged onto the needle before a coagulation tube can contaminate and invalidate clotting results. The order of draw sequences tubes so that carryover cannot corrupt the tests most sensitive to it.

note.t: A single out-of-order EDTA draw can produce a critically high potassium on a healthy patient — a false 'panic value' that triggers needless workup.

p: Draw in this fixed sequence. Sterile and additive-free tubes come first so nothing contaminates them; the strongest, most contaminating additives (EDTA, then fluoride) come last.
list: 1. Blood culture / sterile tubes — first, to protect sterility.
2. Light-blue sodium citrate — coagulation.
3. Serum tubes — red (no additive), then gold / SST.
4. Green heparin — plasma (PST).
5. Lavender / EDTA — hematology.
6. Gray sodium fluoride — glucose / lactate.

note.t: EDTA is drawn near the end and gray last on purpose — their additives are the most damaging if carried into other tubes.

p: A winged (butterfly) set has a length of tubing that holds air — a dead space. On a coagulation-only draw where the light-blue tube is first, that air would be pulled into the citrate tube and short-fill it, breaking the critical 9:1 ratio.

The fix: draw a discard tube first to prime the tubing and remove the dead space. The discard tube can be a plain non-additive or another citrate tube; it is not sent for testing — it just fills the line so your citrate tube draws to its full, correct volume.

note.t: You only need the discard tube to displace the tubing's air — it does not have to fill completely.

inter.q: Tap the tubes into the correct CLSI order of draw, first to last.
inter.fbOk: Correct — sterile first, then citrate, serum, heparin, EDTA, and fluoride last, so no additive is carried into a tube it would corrupt.

tips: Memorize the order by its logic: sterile first, most-contaminating additives last.
When a butterfly is used for a coagulation-only draw, draw a discard tube first to prime the tubing.
Lay your tubes out in order before you stick, so you are not fumbling with a needle in the vein.
mistakes: Drawing EDTA before the coagulation or chemistry tubes.
Skipping the discard tube on a butterfly coag-only draw and short-filling the citrate.
Drawing the gray fluoride tube before EDTA.
Filling a blood culture after additive tubes and contaminating it.
takeaways: Order: culture, blue citrate, red/gold serum, green heparin, lavender EDTA, gray fluoride.
The sequence prevents additive carryover between tubes.
EDTA carryover falsely raises potassium and lowers calcium.
Butterfly coag-only draw: pull a discard tube first to fill the dead space.

quiz.q: Which tube is drawn first in the CLSI order of draw?
quiz.why: Sterile tubes go first so no additive or skin flora contaminates the culture.

quiz.q: What error does EDTA carryover into a chemistry tube cause?
opts: Falsely high potassium and falsely low calcium
quiz.why: EDTA is potassium-based and binds calcium, so carryover raises potassium and lowers calcium.

quiz.q: During a butterfly coagulation-only draw, why draw a discard tube first?
opts: To fill the tubing's air dead space so the citrate tube fills to the correct 9:1 volume
quiz.why: The tubing holds air that would short-fill the first citrate tube and break the 9:1 ratio.

lessons.title: Patient identification & preparation
lessons.lead: The single most dangerous error in phlebotomy is drawing the wrong patient. Everything downstream — the label, the result, the treatment — rides on getting identity right before the needle is anywhere near the arm.
objectives: Identify a patient actively using two independent identifiers matched against the requisition and wristband or ID
Confirm required pre-draw preparation such as fasting or timed collection
Position the patient safely and screen for fainting and relevant allergies
Perform hand hygiene, glove, and explain the procedure to reduce anxiety

p: Identify the patient actively: have them state their full name and date of birth in their own words. Never ask a leading question like "Are you Mr. Smith?" — a drowsy, anxious, or hard-of-hearing patient will nod to anything.

Match those two independent identifiers against the requisition and against a second source: the wristband for an inpatient, or a photo ID (or having the patient state it) for an outpatient. All sources must agree before you proceed.
list: Identifier 1: full legal name.
Identifier 2: date of birth.
Match against the requisition AND the wristband (inpatient) or photo ID / patient statement (outpatient).

note.t: If any identifier does not match — a nickname, a wrong birth year, a missing wristband — stop and resolve the discrepancy before drawing. Do not label from memory.

p: Some tests are only valid under specific conditions. Confirm the patient met them before you draw, and note any deviation so the lab can interpret the result.

Fasting is required for tests such as fasting glucose and a lipid panel (typically 8–12 hours, water permitted). Timing matters for drug levels and other timed collections — a therapeutic drug level drawn at the wrong time is worse than useless.
list: Fasting glucose and lipid panel — confirm the fasting window was kept.
Therapeutic drug monitoring — confirm peak vs. trough timing.
Any timed test — record the actual collection time.

note.t: Ask "When did you last eat or drink anything besides water?" rather than "Are you fasting?" — you get a truthful answer instead of a guess.

p: Seat the patient with the arm supported and extended slightly downward, or place them supine. Never draw a patient perched on a stool, standing, or in a chair they could fall out of.

Ask about prior fainting during blood draws; a patient at risk of syncope should be reclined or supine, never drawn standing. Check for latex and adhesive allergies before choosing gloves and bandage. Perform hand hygiene, then glove, and briefly explain what you are about to do — a calm explanation lowers anxiety and the vasovagal risk that comes with it.

note.t: A history of fainting is a red flag: recline the patient first. A syncopal episode with a needle in the arm can cause serious injury.

inter.case: You approach an inpatient with a requisition for a metabolic panel. The patient looks sleepy.
inter.q: What is the correct way to confirm you have the right patient?

opts.lab: Ask "You're Mrs. Johnson, right?" and proceed when she nods
opts.fb: No — a leading question invites a false yes. A drowsy patient may agree to any name.

opts.lab: Have her state her full name and date of birth, and match both to the requisition and wristband
opts.fb: Correct — two independent identifiers, stated actively and matched against the requisition and the wristband.

opts.lab: Check the wristband alone since it is the official record
opts.fb: Not enough — the band must be matched against what the patient states and the requisition; bands can be mixed up.

tips: Have the patient spell an unusual name; it catches label errors before they happen.
Ask about the fasting window in plain language — "when did you last eat?" — not yes/no.
Recline any patient who reports a history of fainting before you touch the arm.
mistakes: Asking a leading question like "Are you Mr. Smith?" instead of having the patient state their name.
Using only one identifier, or trusting the wristband without matching the requisition.
Drawing a patient standing or on a high stool despite a fainting history.
Skipping the fasting or timing check and invalidating the result.
takeaways: Two independent identifiers — full name and date of birth — stated actively and matched to requisition plus wristband or ID.
Confirm fasting and timing before you draw.
Screen for fainting and allergies; position and recline for safety.
Hand hygiene, then gloves, then a calm explanation.

quiz.q: Which is an acceptable pair of independent identifiers?
opts: Full name and date of birth
quiz.why: Full name and date of birth are two independent, patient-specific identifiers required for active identification.

quiz.q: How should you confirm a patient's identity?
opts: Ask them to confirm the name you read aloud
Have them state their name and date of birth in their own words
quiz.why: Active identification means the patient states their identifiers; you never lead with the name.

quiz.q: A patient reports fainting at their last blood draw. What do you do?
opts: Draw quickly while they are seated upright
Recline or lay the patient supine before drawing
quiz.why: A syncope history calls for a reclined or supine position to prevent injury from fainting.

lessons.refs: CLSI GP41 (2017); ASCP/NAACLS competencies; The Joint Commission NPSG.01.01.01.

lessons.title: Site selection & the tourniquet
lessons.lead: The tourniquet and the alcohol prep are where good technique is won or lost. A tourniquet left on too long or an arm chosen without checking history can turn a clean draw into a bad result — or harm.
objectives: Apply and time the tourniquet correctly to avoid hemoconcentration
Palpate to select a springy, non-pulsatile vein
Cleanse the site with 70% isopropyl alcohol and let it air-dry
Recognize arms and sites that must be avoided

sections.h: The tourniquet: placement and the one-minute rule
p: Apply the tourniquet 3–4 inches (7.5–10 cm) above the intended puncture site — snug enough to distend the veins but not so tight it obstructs arterial flow. It should be easy to release with one pull.

Leave it on no more than 1 minute. Prolonged application causes hemoconcentration — plasma leaves the vessel and cell-bound and protein-bound analytes falsely rise. If you need more time to find a vein, release and reapply after a short pause.

note.t: Beyond a minute, hemostasis under the tourniquet concentrates the sample and falsely elevates results such as potassium, total protein, and calcium.

sections.h: Palpate, then cleanse and let it dry
p: Palpate with a fingertip to locate the vein and confirm it is springy and non-pulsatile — a pulsating vessel is an artery; do not stick it. Note its depth and direction.

Cleanse with 70% isopropyl alcohol in a circular, outward motion from the center, and then let it air-dry. Wet alcohol stings on entry and hemolyzes the sample. Do not re-palpate the cleaned site; if you must touch it again, re-cleanse first.
list: Palpate to confirm a springy, non-pulsatile vein.
Cleanse with 70% isopropyl alcohol, circular and outward.
Let the site air-dry completely before puncture.
Do not re-palpate the cleaned site (or re-cleanse if you do).

note.t: Give the alcohol 30 seconds to dry. If you are tempted to fan or blow on it, don't — that recontaminates the site.

p: Some sites raise the risk of a false result or real harm. Choose a different arm or site — or get provider permission — when any of the following apply.
list: Same side as a mastectomy (lymphedema and infection risk).
An arm with an active IV or infusion — use the other arm, or draw well below the IV if there is no alternative.
A hematoma, or scarred, burned, or heavily tattooed skin.
Edematous (swollen) tissue — the fluid dilutes the sample.
An AV fistula or graft — never apply a tourniquet or draw there.
Foot or ankle veins require provider permission.

note.t: Drawing above an IV pulls infusing fluid into your sample and drawing from a fistula can damage a dialysis patient's access — both are avoidable errors.

inter.case: You have been searching for a good vein and the tourniquet has been on for about 90 seconds.
inter.q: What should you do before drawing?

opts.lab: Draw now — the vein is finally standing up
opts.fb: No — beyond one minute the sample is hemoconcentrated and several analytes will read falsely high.

opts.lab: Release the tourniquet, wait a couple of minutes, then reapply and draw
opts.fb: Correct — releasing and reapplying resets the one-minute window and prevents hemoconcentration.

opts.lab: Loosen it slightly but keep it in place to save time
opts.fb: Not enough — the blood is already concentrated; you must fully release and pause before reapplying.

tips: Anchor the tourniquet with a quick-release tuck so one pull frees it.
If a vein won't come up, warm the site or lower the arm instead of leaving the tourniquet on.
Cleanse in one direction, center outward, and let the alcohol dry on its own.
mistakes: Leaving the tourniquet on longer than a minute and hemoconcentrating the sample.
Puncturing before the alcohol dries, causing stinging and hemolysis.
Re-palpating the cleaned site with a bare finger.
Drawing from an arm with an IV, a fistula, or on the mastectomy side.
takeaways: Tourniquet 3–4 inches above the site, on for no more than one minute.
Palpate for a springy, non-pulsatile vein.
70% isopropyl alcohol, circular and outward, then air-dry.
Avoid the mastectomy side, IV arm, hematoma, scarred/tattooed skin, edema, and AV access.

quiz.q: How far above the site should the tourniquet go?
quiz.why: Placing it 3–4 inches above distends the veins without occluding arterial flow.

quiz.q: Why must the alcohol air-dry before puncture?
opts: Wet alcohol stings and hemolyzes the sample
To make the vein easier to see
quiz.why: Entering through wet alcohol causes patient stinging and hemolysis of the specimen.

quiz.q: Which arm should you avoid drawing from?
opts: The arm on the same side as a mastectomy
quiz.why: The post-mastectomy side carries lymphedema and infection risk and should be avoided.

lessons.title: Venipuncture technique
lessons.lead: Once identity, site, and prep are set, the puncture itself is a short, ordered sequence. Do the steps in the right order and the draw is smooth, safe, and clean; skip or reorder one and you risk a blown vein, a hemolyzed sample, or a needlestick.
objectives: Insert the needle bevel-up at a controlled angle after anchoring the vein
Fill and change tubes correctly, respecting the order of draw and additive mixing
Release the tourniquet before withdrawing the needle
Withdraw safely, activate the safety device, and secure hemostasis

p: Position the needle bevel up. Anchor the skin taut with your thumb 1–2 inches below the site to stop the vein rolling, and keep your thumb below and away from the needle path.
Insert in one smooth motion at a 15–30° angle to the skin. A shallow, deliberate entry finds the lumen cleanly; a steep or hesitant jab pushes through the back wall.

note.t: A small flash of blood in the hub confirms you are in the vein. Hold the needle still once you see it.

p: Seat the tube onto the needle in the holder and let the vacuum fill it fully — don't pull the tube off early. Fill citrate (light-blue) tubes completely to preserve the 9:1 blood-to-additive ratio; an underfilled coagulation tube gives falsely prolonged times.
Change tubes following the order of draw, and invert additive tubes gently the required number of times immediately after filling. Do not shake — vigorous mixing hemolyzes the sample.

note.t: The 9:1 ratio in a citrate tube is calibrated for a full draw; short-filling changes the ratio and skews PT/INR and aPTT.

p: Release the tourniquet before you withdraw the needle — and before it has been on a full minute. Withdrawing against a tight tourniquet forces blood out of the site.

Place gauze over the site without pressing, withdraw the needle smoothly, and immediately activate the needle safety device. Then apply firm pressure with the arm held straight — not bent, which reopens the puncture and bruises — until bleeding stops, and bandage.

note.t: Activate the safety device the instant the needle clears the skin. The window between withdrawal and activation is when most needlesticks happen.

inter.q: Tap the steps into the correct order for a routine venipuncture.

items.txt: Fill tubes in order of draw

inter.fbOk: Exactly right — anchor, enter, fill, release the tourniquet, withdraw over gauze, activate the safety, then pressure and bandage.

tips: Keep the needle still while tubes change; movement in the vein is what bruises.
Invert additive tubes as you go rather than saving them all for the end.
Have the gauze ready in your free hand before you withdraw.
mistakes: Inserting bevel-down or at too steep an angle and hitting the back wall.
Underfilling a citrate tube and ruining the 9:1 ratio.
Withdrawing the needle before releasing the tourniquet.
Failing to activate the safety device immediately, risking a needlestick.
takeaways: Bevel up, anchor taut, insert at 15–30° in one motion.
Fill tubes fully in order of draw and invert additive tubes gently.
Release the tourniquet before withdrawing the needle.
Withdraw over gauze, activate the safety, then firm pressure on a straight arm.

quiz.q: At what angle should the needle enter the skin?
quiz.why: A 15–30° angle enters the lumen cleanly without punching through the far wall.

quiz.q: When should the tourniquet be released?
opts: It is left on until bandaging
quiz.why: Releasing before withdrawal prevents blood being forced out of the puncture and limits hemoconcentration.

quiz.q: What must you do immediately after the needle clears the skin?
quiz.why: Immediate safety activation closes the window when most accidental needlesticks occur.

lessons.refs: CLSI GP41 (2017); OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard; ASCP.

lessons.title: Complications & how to respond
lessons.lead: Most draws are uneventful, but the ones that aren't demand a fast, correct response. Knowing the difference between a bruise and a nerve injury — and what to do in the next few seconds — is what separates a competent phlebotomist from a dangerous one.
objectives: Recognize and respond to hematoma, hemolysis, and nerve injury
Manage vasovagal syncope and protect a fainting patient
Apply the two-attempt rule and know when to escalate
Identify an arterial puncture and respond correctly

p: A hematoma — swelling and blood leaking under the skin — means the vessel is compromised. Release the tourniquet, remove the needle, and apply firm pressure until it stops. Do not keep advancing.

Hemolysis ruptures red cells and spills their contents into the plasma, falsely elevating potassium, LDH, and other intracellular analytes. Its common causes are avoidable: a too-small needle with syringe force, vigorous shaking or mixing, drawing through a hematoma, puncturing through wet alcohol, and underfilling an additive tube. Petechiae — tiny red spots — can appear from tourniquet pressure or a clotting problem and warn that bleeding may be prolonged.
list: Hematoma: release tourniquet, remove needle, firm pressure.
Hemolysis causes: small needle + syringe force, shaking, drawing through a hematoma, wet alcohol, underfilled additive tube.
Hemolysis effect: falsely elevated potassium, LDH, and similar analytes.

note.t: A hemolyzed potassium can read dangerously high and trigger unnecessary treatment — a preventable error that starts at the needle.

p: If the patient feels sudden sharp, shooting, or electric pain, or numbness radiating down the arm, you may have contacted a nerve — remove the needle immediately and select a new site. Do not reposition and dig.

Vasovagal syncope (fainting) can come on fast: pallor, sweating, lightheadedness. Stop the draw, lower the patient's head, apply a cold compress, and stay with them — never leave a fainting patient alone. Protect them from falling and keep the airway clear.

note.t: Shooting or electric pain is a nerve warning, not a normal stick. The needle comes out at once — pushing on risks lasting nerve damage.

sections.h: Over-drawing, the two-attempt rule, and arterial puncture
p: Repeated or high-volume draws cause iatrogenic anemia, especially in small or frequently tested patients — take only what is needed. Follow the two-attempt rule: no more than two attempts, then escalate to a colleague or the phlebotomy/vascular access team rather than sticking again.

Arterial puncture shows bright-red, pulsating blood that fills the tube rapidly. Remove the needle and hold firm pressure for at least 5 minutes, then notify the appropriate staff and document. Confirm bleeding has fully stopped before the patient leaves.

note.t: Two attempts is the ceiling, not a target. Escalating is a sign of good judgment, not failure.

inter.case: As you advance the needle, the patient cries out with sharp electric pain shooting toward the hand.

opts.lab: Reposition the needle slightly and continue the draw
opts.fb: No — probing near a nerve risks lasting injury. The needle must come out.

opts.lab: Remove the needle immediately and choose a new site
opts.fb: Correct — sharp, shooting, electric pain signals nerve contact; withdraw at once.

opts.lab: Ask the patient to tolerate it since the tube is nearly full
opts.fb: No — nerve pain is never something to push through; withdraw immediately.

tips: Watch the patient's face, not just the tube — pallor and sweat precede a faint.
Keep a cold compress within reach for the first sign of syncope.
If the first two sticks fail, hand off; a fresh set of eyes finds the vein.
Bright-red pulsating blood means artery — pressure for at least five minutes.
mistakes: Advancing or repositioning the needle after the patient reports shooting pain.
Shaking additive tubes or drawing through a hematoma, causing hemolysis.
Leaving a fainting patient alone to get help.
Making a third, fourth, or fifth attempt instead of escalating.
takeaways: Hematoma: release tourniquet, remove needle, firm pressure.
Shooting/electric pain: remove the needle immediately.
Fainting: stop, lower the head, cold compress, and never leave the patient.
Two attempts maximum; arterial puncture means at least 5 minutes of pressure and notify.

quiz.q: A patient reports sudden electric, shooting pain down the arm during insertion. What do you do?
quiz.why: Shooting or electric pain signals nerve contact and requires immediate needle removal.

quiz.q: Which finding indicates an arterial puncture?
quiz.why: Arterial blood is bright red and pulsates, filling the tube rapidly; hold pressure at least 5 minutes.

quiz.q: After two unsuccessful attempts, what is the correct action?
opts: Try a third time on the other arm
Escalate to a colleague or the vascular access team
quiz.why: The two-attempt rule caps attempts at two; beyond that you escalate rather than repeat.

lessons.title: Capillary (dermal) puncture
lessons.lead: When a full venous draw isn't needed or isn't possible — a fingerstick glucose, a tiny infant, or veins you simply can't reach — a capillary puncture is the answer. But the site, the depth, and even the order of collection are different, and getting them wrong can injure a patient or ruin the sample.
objectives: Identify when a capillary puncture is indicated
Select the correct site for adults and for infants
Perform the puncture with correct depth and technique
Collect in the capillary order and avoid tissue-fluid contamination

sections.h: When to use it, and where
p: Capillary (dermal) puncture suits point-of-care glucose, small-volume tests, infants and young children, and patients with difficult venous access. It yields a mix of capillary, venous, and arterial blood plus tissue fluid.

For an adult or older child, use the palmar surface of the distal (last) segment of the middle or ring finger, off to the side of center — not the very tip and not the side of the finger. For an infant under 1 year, use the medial or lateral plantar surface of the heel only.
list: Indications: POC glucose, small volume, infants/children, difficult venous access.
Adult/older child: side of center of the last segment of the middle or ring finger.
Infant (<1 yr): medial or lateral plantar heel surface only.

note.t: Never puncture the center or arch of an infant's heel, the back of the heel, or a previous site — the bone is close beneath and you risk osteomyelitis and nerve injury.

sections.h: Depth, warming, and the first drop
p: Keep the puncture depth under 2.0 mm in an infant to stay clear of bone. Warm the site (a warm cloth for a few minutes) to increase blood flow and make collection easier.

After the puncture, wipe away the first drop — it is contaminated with tissue fluid and skews results. Do not strongly milk or squeeze the finger or heel; excessive pressure causes hemolysis and tissue-fluid contamination. Gentle, intermittent pressure with the site held downward gives the best drops.

note.t: Warming can roughly double capillary flow — a minute with a warm compress often saves you from squeezing.

sections.h: The capillary order of collection is reversed
p: Because a dermal puncture starts to clot quickly, the collection order is different from — essentially the reverse of — the venous order of draw. Collect the tests most sensitive to clotting and platelet clumping first.
Collect EDTA (hematology) tubes first, then other additive tubes, then serum tubes last. This captures platelets and cell counts before clotting begins and distorts them.
list: 1. EDTA (hematology) first.
2. Other additive tubes.
3. Serum tubes last.

note.t: Capillary blood clots fast, so EDTA goes first — the opposite of venous order — to protect the platelet count and CBC from clumping.

inter.case: You need a small blood sample from a 3-month-old for a bilirubin level.

opts.lab: The center (arch) of the heel
opts.fb: No — the center and arch sit over bone; puncturing there risks nerve and bone injury.

opts.lab: The medial or lateral plantar surface of the heel
opts.fb: Correct — the side portions of the plantar heel are the only safe sites in an infant under one year.

opts.lab: The tip of the big toe
opts.fb: No — the toe is not a recommended capillary site; use the medial or lateral plantar heel.

tips: Warm the site before you puncture; it beats squeezing every time.
Always wipe away the first drop before you start filling.
Hold the finger or heel downward and use gentle, intermittent pressure.
mistakes: Puncturing the center or arch of an infant's heel, or a previous site.
Squeezing hard, which hemolyzes the sample and adds tissue fluid.
Including the first drop instead of wiping it away.
Collecting in venous order instead of EDTA-first for capillary.
takeaways: Capillary puncture for POC glucose, small volumes, infants, and difficult access.
Adult: side of center of the last segment of the middle or ring finger. Infant: medial/lateral plantar heel, depth < 2.0 mm.
Warm the site, wipe the first drop, do not milk hard.
Capillary order is reversed — EDTA first, additives next, serum last.

quiz.q: Where do you perform a capillary puncture on an adult?
opts: The very tip of the index finger
The side of center of the last segment of the middle or ring finger
quiz.why: The distal segment of the middle or ring finger, off to the side of center, is the standard adult dermal site.

quiz.q: Why is the first drop of blood wiped away?
opts: It is contaminated with tissue fluid
quiz.why: The first drop contains tissue fluid that would skew the results.

quiz.q: What is collected first in a capillary draw?
quiz.why: Capillary blood clots quickly, so EDTA is collected first to protect the cell counts — the reverse of venous order.

lessons.title: Special & difficult draws
lessons.lead: The routine draw you have practiced changes at the extremes of age and in patients whose veins fight you. Adjusting your equipment, angle, and approach — and knowing when to escalate — is what keeps these draws safe and successful.
objectives: Adapt technique for pediatric and geriatric patients
Manage obese, edematous, and dehydrated patients
Collect blood cultures with strict aseptic technique
Handle fasting, timed, and therapeutic drug monitoring draws and escalate difficult access

p: For pediatric patients, use a winged (butterfly) set and smaller-volume tubes, employ comfort holds and distraction, follow the same order of draw, and watch the total volume drawn against the child's size to avoid iatrogenic anemia.

Geriatric patients have fragile, rolling veins and thin skin. Anchor the vein well, use a lower insertion angle and less tourniquet tension, and consider a butterfly for better control. Excess tourniquet pressure can rupture a fragile vein before you even enter it.

note.t: A butterfly set with lighter tourniquet tension gives you the control that fragile pediatric and geriatric veins demand.

p: In obese patients veins are deep and hard to palpate — rely on feel over sight and take time to map the vein. In edematous tissue, avoid the swollen area entirely; the fluid dilutes the sample and the vein is displaced.
Dehydrated patients have collapsed, poorly filling veins. Warming, hydration where appropriate, and gravity (lowering the arm) help, but do not chase a vein with repeated blind sticks.
list: Obese: palpate carefully; veins are deep, not always visible.
Edematous: avoid the swollen tissue — it dilutes the sample.
Dehydrated: expect collapsed veins; warm, position, and don't stick blindly.

note.t: Never draw through edematous tissue — the interstitial fluid contaminates the specimen and the underlying vein is displaced and easily missed.

p: Blood cultures demand strict aseptic preparation: cleanse thoroughly, let it dry, and do not re-touch the site. Collect the correct volume into the aerobic and anaerobic bottles and typically draw from two sites to distinguish true infection from contamination.

Fasting, timed, and therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) draws hinge on timing. TDM distinguishes a peak (drawn after a dose reaches maximum concentration) from a trough (drawn just before the next dose). Draw at the ordered time and record it. When access is genuinely difficult, escalate rather than repeat blind attempts.

note.t: Re-touching a prepped blood-culture site is the classic source of a contaminated culture — a false positive that can mean days of unnecessary antibiotics.

inter.case: An elderly patient has thin skin and veins that roll under your finger.
inter.q: How do you adjust your technique?

opts.lab: Apply a tighter tourniquet and use a steeper angle to catch the vein fast
opts.fb: No — high tension and a steep angle can rupture a fragile vein and blow the stick.

opts.lab: Anchor well, lower the angle, reduce tourniquet tension, and consider a butterfly
opts.fb: Correct — anchoring, a shallow angle, and gentle tension protect fragile rolling veins; a butterfly adds control.

opts.lab: Skip the tourniquet entirely and rely on gravity alone
opts.fb: Not quite — some light tension still helps; the key is less tension, better anchoring, and a lower angle.

tips: Reach for a butterfly and smaller tubes when veins are fragile or small.
Distraction and a comfortable hold make pediatric draws faster and calmer.
For blood cultures, prep, let dry, and never re-palpate the site.
Confirm whether a drug level is a peak or a trough before you draw.
mistakes: Using full tourniquet tension and a steep angle on a fragile geriatric vein.
Drawing through edematous tissue and diluting the sample.
Re-touching a prepped blood-culture site and contaminating it.
Repeating blind sticks on difficult access instead of escalating.
takeaways: Pediatric: butterfly, small tubes, comfort holds, watch total volume.
Geriatric: anchor well, lower angle, less tourniquet tension, consider a butterfly.
Avoid edematous tissue; palpate carefully in obese and dehydrated patients.
Blood cultures: strict asepsis, no re-touch, two sites; know peak vs. trough; escalate difficult access.

quiz.q: What is the best approach for a fragile, rolling geriatric vein?
opts: Anchor well, lower angle, less tourniquet tension
quiz.why: Good anchoring, a shallow angle, and gentle tension protect fragile veins and reduce rupture.

quiz.q: Why must you not re-touch a prepped blood-culture site?
opts: It contaminates the culture and causes false positives
quiz.why: Re-palpating a disinfected site reintroduces skin flora and is a leading cause of contaminated cultures.

quiz.q: A trough drug level is drawn when?
opts: Right after the dose is given
quiz.why: A trough is the lowest concentration, drawn immediately before the next dose.

lessons.refs: CLSI GP41 (2017); CLSI GP42 (2020); ASCP/NAACLS competencies.

lessons.title: Labeling, handling & transport
lessons.lead: A perfect stick is wasted if the tube is mislabeled, shaken, or left to sit. What you do in the 60 seconds after the needle comes out decides whether the lab can trust the result.
objectives: Label every tube at the bedside, in the patient's presence, immediately after collection
State the required label elements and mix additive tubes correctly
Apply handling rules for light, temperature, and clotting
Recognize the specimen rejection criteria that force a redraw

sections.h: Label at the bedside — every time
p: Label the tubes at the bedside, immediately, in the patient's presence — before you leave the room and before you do anything else. Never pre-label empty tubes and never label away from the patient. Pre-labeling and hallway labeling are the two habits behind most wrong-patient errors.

Confirm identity against the label using two identifiers, and let the patient confirm their name and date of birth if able. The label ties this blood to this person; get it wrong and every downstream result is dangerous.
list: Patient full name
ID / MRN (medical record number)
Date of birth
Date and time of collection
The collector's initials

note.t: If you cannot label at the bedside in the patient's presence, do not collect. An unlabeled tube leaving the room is a wrong-patient event waiting to happen.

p: Additive tubes must be mixed right after filling: gently invert 8–10 times, a smooth end-over-end motion. Never shake — shaking hemolyzes the sample and ruptures cells, wrecking chemistry and hematology results.

Some specimens need protection. Shield light-sensitive analytes such as bilirubin from light. Honor temperature requirements — a few specimens go on ice while others must be kept warm — and let serum tubes clot fully (about 30 minutes) before you centrifuge them.
list: Invert additive tubes 8–10 times, gently — no shaking.
Protect light-sensitive specimens (e.g. bilirubin) from light.
Follow temperature rules: some on ice, some kept warm.
Let serum tubes clot ~30 min before centrifuging.

note.t: Vigorous shaking and incomplete clotting are leading causes of hemolysis and fibrin strands — both trigger a redraw.

p: The lab will reject a specimen it cannot trust, and a rejection means a redraw and a delayed result. Knowing the criteria lets you prevent them at the chair instead of hearing about them an hour later.
list: Unlabeled or mislabeled tube — the number-one cause.
Hemolyzed specimen (from shaking, a small needle, or vigorous draw).
Clotted EDTA / hematology tube (poor mixing).
Wrong tube or wrong additive for the test ordered.
Quantity not sufficient (QNS) — underfilled tube.
An expired tube (past its expiration date).

note.t: Check the tube expiration date before you fill it — an expired tube's additive and vacuum can no longer be trusted.

inter.case: You have just filled a lavender-top EDTA tube for a CBC at the bedside.
inter.q: What do you do next, before leaving the room?

opts.lab: Shake the tube hard to mix the additive, then label it in the hallway
opts.fb: Two errors: shaking hemolyzes the sample, and hallway labeling risks a wrong-patient mix-up.

opts.lab: Gently invert it 8–10 times and label it at the bedside in the patient's presence
opts.fb: Correct — gentle inversion mixes the anticoagulant without hemolysis, and bedside labeling ties the tube to the patient.

opts.lab: Set it in the rack unmixed and label all your tubes together at the nurses' station
opts.fb: An EDTA tube left unmixed clots and is rejected, and station labeling breaks the chain of identity.

tips: Say the patient's name and DOB aloud as you write the label — it catches mismatches.
Invert immediately after each additive tube fills, while you are still gowned up.
Wrap bilirubin and other light-sensitive tubes in foil or use an amber transport sleeve.
mistakes: Pre-labeling empty tubes before the draw.
Shaking additive tubes instead of gently inverting.
Centrifuging a serum tube before it has clotted ~30 minutes.
Sending an underfilled (QNS) coagulation tube.
takeaways: Label at the bedside, in the patient's presence, immediately — never pre-label.
Gentle inversion 8–10 times; never shake.
Protect light-sensitive and temperature-sensitive specimens; clot serum ~30 min.
Unlabeled, hemolyzed, clotted, wrong-tube, QNS, or expired = rejected.

quiz.q: When and where should blood tubes be labeled?
opts: Pre-labeled before the draw for speed
At the bedside, immediately, in the patient's presence
quiz.why: Bedside labeling in the patient's presence is the safeguard against wrong-patient errors.

quiz.q: How should an additive tube be mixed after filling?
opts: Leave it still so cells settle
quiz.why: Gentle inversion 8–10 times mixes the additive without causing hemolysis.

quiz.q: Which of these is a standard specimen rejection criterion?
opts: A tube filled to the correct volume
quiz.why: A clotted EDTA tube cannot yield an accurate CBC and is rejected for a redraw.

lessons.refs: CLSI GP41 (2017); CLSI H18 (specimen handling); ASCP phlebotomy competencies.

lessons.title: Safety, exposure & quality
lessons.lead: The riskiest moment of a draw is often after the blood is in the tube — when a bare needle is still in your hand. Safe device handling and a clear exposure plan protect you as much as the specimen protects the patient.
objectives: Activate the safety device and dispose of sharps without recapping
Name the major bloodborne pathogens and apply standard precautions
Follow the needlestick / exposure protocol step by step
Connect QA/QC and technique to prevention of pre-analytical errors

p: The instant the needle leaves the vein, activate the needle safety device — the shield or blunting mechanism — and never recap a needle. Recapping is when most accidental sticks happen, and it is prohibited by standard precautions.

Dispose of the sharp immediately into a puncture-resistant sharps container. Do not walk around with a used needle, do not set it down, and do not overfill the container — replace it when it reaches the fill line.

note.t: Recapping a needle is a leading cause of needlestick injury. Engage the safety device before the needle ever moves toward a cap.

p: Blood can transmit bloodborne pathogens — most importantly hepatitis B (HBV), hepatitis C (HCV), and HIV. Under standard precautions, you treat every patient's blood and body fluids as potentially infectious, regardless of their known status.
That means gloves for every draw, hand hygiene before and after, and personal protective equipment appropriate to the risk. Standard precautions protect you, the patient, and everyone downstream.
list: Perform hand hygiene and wear gloves for every patient.
Treat all blood and body fluids as infectious.
Use engineered safety devices and dispose of sharps at once.
Know that HBV vaccination is recommended for anyone handling blood.

note.t: HBV survives on surfaces and is far more transmissible per exposure than HIV — which is exactly why no shortcut on precautions is acceptable.

p: A needlestick or blood splash is an emergency you can manage if you act fast. Wash the area immediately — flush a puncture wound with soap and water, flush mucous membranes with water or saline — then report it right away to your supervisor and employee health.

Follow the post-exposure evaluation: the source patient and the exposed worker are assessed, and post-exposure prophylaxis is started quickly when indicated. Reporting late narrows the window in which prophylaxis works.
list: Wash the wound with soap and water (flush mucous membranes with water/saline).
Report immediately to your supervisor and employee/occupational health.
Follow the post-exposure evaluation and prophylaxis protocol.
Document the exposure and the source, per facility policy.

note.t: Post-exposure prophylaxis is time-sensitive. Never hide or delay an exposure — reporting fast is what protects you.

p: Quality assurance (QA) is the whole system that keeps results trustworthy; quality control (QC) is the day-to-day checks — expiration dates, equipment function, and technique — that keep the system honest. Most lab errors are pre-analytical: they happen before the specimen is ever tested, in identification, collection, and handling.

Correct technique and specimen integrity are how you prevent those errors. So is professional documentation and accountability — recording what you did, owning a mistake, and reporting it so it can be fixed rather than repeated.

note.t: When something goes wrong, document it and speak up. Most pre-analytical errors are preventable, and honest reporting is how a lab stops them recurring.

inter.case: You have finished a draw. The needle is out of the arm and still uncapped in your hand.
inter.q: What is the correct next action?

opts.lab: Carefully recap the needle so it is safe to carry to the sharps bin
opts.fb: Recapping is prohibited — it is exactly the moment most needlesticks occur.

opts.lab: Activate the safety device and drop it straight into the sharps container
opts.fb: Correct — engage the safety shield immediately and dispose of the sharp at once, without recapping.

opts.lab: Set the needle on the tray while you label the tubes, then bin it
opts.fb: Never set down an unguarded sharp — activate the safety device and dispose of it immediately.

tips: Position the sharps container within arm's reach before you start the draw.
Engage the safety device with one motion, away from your other hand.
Know where your facility's exposure report and employee-health line are before you ever need them.
mistakes: Recapping a used needle.
Carrying an unguarded sharp across the room.
Delaying or not reporting a needlestick.
Skipping gloves or hand hygiene because the patient 'looks healthy'.
takeaways: Activate the safety device and never recap; bin sharps immediately.
HBV, HCV, HIV — apply standard precautions to everyone.
Exposure: wash, report immediately, follow post-exposure evaluation.
Most lab errors are pre-analytical; technique, QC, and honest documentation prevent them.

quiz.q: What should you never do with a used needle?
opts: Drop it in a sharps container
quiz.why: Recapping is a leading cause of needlestick injury and is prohibited under standard precautions.

quiz.q: Which set of pathogens is the main bloodborne concern in phlebotomy?
quiz.why: Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV are the primary bloodborne pathogens transmitted by blood exposure.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do after a needlestick injury?
opts: Finish your shift, then mention it later
Wash the area and report the exposure immediately
Recap the needle and reuse a fresh one
quiz.why: Washing the wound and reporting at once preserves the time-sensitive window for post-exposure prophylaxis.

lessons.refs: OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard 29 CFR 1910.1030; CDC post-exposure guidance; CLSI GP41 (2017); ASCP.

lessons.title: Putting it together
lessons.lead: Real draws rarely test one skill at a time. Here you'll work three short cases that fold identification, order of draw, complications, and special populations into single decisions — the way a real chair-side shift does.
objectives: Integrate order of draw and fill requirements in a multi-tube collection
Respond correctly to a complication that develops mid-draw
Apply site-selection rules for patients with restricted arms
Reason through combined identification, technique, and special-population decisions

sections.h: Case A — Fasting glucose and a coag panel
p: A fasting adult is ordered a glucose (gray-top, sodium fluoride/potassium oxalate) and a coagulation panel (light-blue, sodium citrate). You will draw both from one clean venipuncture. The question is sequence and fill.

By the order of draw, the light-blue coagulation tube comes before the gray tube: blood cultures, then light-blue (citrate), then serum, then green, then lavender, then gray last. The light-blue tube must fill completely to keep the exact 9:1 blood-to-citrate ratio — an underfilled coag tube is rejected.

note.t: Draw the light-blue citrate tube before the gray tube, and fill it to the line — the coagulation result depends on the 9:1 ratio.

sections.h: Case B — The patient goes pale mid-draw
p: Halfway through the draw your patient goes quiet, pale, and sweaty and says she feels lightheaded. This is a vasovagal (syncope) reaction starting. Act before she loses consciousness.

Remove the tourniquet and needle immediately, apply pressure to the site, and protect her from falling — lower the head or lay her down, and never leave her alone. Cool compress, reassurance, and keeping her seated or reclined until fully recovered come next. Only resume or reschedule once she is stable.

note.t: At the first sign of fainting, the draw stops. Discontinue, protect the airway and prevent a fall — a completed tube is never worth a head injury.

sections.h: Case C — The post-mastectomy patient with an IV arm
p: Your patient had a left mastectomy with lymph node removal, and her right arm has a running IV. Both arms carry a restriction, so site selection is the whole test here.

Avoid the arm on the side of a mastectomy with lymph node dissection — the lymphedema risk makes it off-limits without provider clearance. Avoid drawing above or at an IV; if you must use that arm, draw below the IV site after it has been paused per protocol. Better options: a hand or lower-arm vein on an acceptable site, or escalate to the nurse or provider for guidance.

note.t: Two restricted arms is a stop-and-think, not a guess. When both sides are compromised, get provider guidance rather than forcing a marginal site.

inter.h: One vein, two tubes, a twist
inter.case: A fasting patient needs a light-blue coagulation tube and a gray glucose tube. You get a single clean flash in the median cubital, but the vein is small and flow is slow — the light-blue tube is filling sluggishly and stops just short of the line.

opts.lab: Send the short-filled light-blue tube anyway and note it was a hard stick
opts.fb: No — an underfilled citrate tube breaks the 9:1 ratio and will be rejected, delaying the coag result.

opts.lab: Top it off from the gray tube so the volume looks right
opts.fb: Never transfer between tubes — it cross-contaminates additives and invalidates both results.

opts.lab: Discontinue and redraw the coag tube with a fresh stick, filling it to the line first in the order of draw
opts.fb: Correct — a coagulation tube must fill completely for a valid ratio; redraw and fill the light-blue tube to the line, before the gray, within the two-attempt limit.

opts.lab: Squeeze and milk the arm hard to force the tube to fill
opts.fb: Vigorous milking hemolyzes the sample and activates clotting factors, ruining a coagulation specimen.

tips: Line up tubes in draw order before you stick so sequence is automatic under pressure.
Watch the patient's face, not just the flash — pallor and sweating warn you before a faint.
When both arms are restricted, escalate early rather than forcing a poor site.
mistakes: Drawing the gray tube before the light-blue coagulation tube.
Sending an underfilled citrate tube instead of redrawing.
Continuing a draw after a patient reports feeling faint.
Using the arm on a mastectomy side or drawing above an IV.
takeaways: Order of draw and full fill protect the coagulation ratio.
First sign of syncope: discontinue, protect from a fall, never leave the patient.
Avoid a mastectomy-side arm and don't draw above an IV.
When variables stack up, stop and reason — or escalate.

quiz.q: Drawing a light-blue coag tube and a gray glucose tube from one stick, which fills first and why?
opts: Gray first, because glucose degrades fastest
Light-blue first, to protect the citrate ratio and avoid additive carryover
Either order — sequence doesn't affect these two
quiz.why: The citrate (light-blue) tube precedes the gray in the order of draw and must fill fully to keep the 9:1 ratio.

quiz.q: A patient becomes pale, sweaty, and lightheaded mid-draw. What is your first action?
opts: Speed up to finish before she faints
Remove the tourniquet and needle, apply pressure, and protect her from falling
Leave to get help, telling her to hold the site
quiz.why: You discontinue immediately and prevent a fall — and you never leave a fainting patient unattended.

quiz.q: A patient had a left mastectomy with node removal and has an IV in the right arm. Where do you draw?
opts: The left arm, since the IV blocks the right
Below the IV on the right after pausing it, or escalate for a cleared site
Above the IV on the right for cleaner flow
quiz.why: The mastectomy side is avoided for lymphedema risk; on the IV arm you draw below a paused IV or get provider guidance.
